The authors of the paper proposed the focal loss function as a solution to the class imbalance problem that is inherent in dense object detection tasks. In dense object detection, the number of background examples (i.e., non-object regions) far exceeds the number of foreground examples (i.e., object regions). This class imbalance can lead to biased models that are overly specialized in detecting background regions, resulting in poor performance on foreground regions. The focal loss function is designed to address this issue by down-weighting the loss contribution from well-classified examples (i.e., background regions) and up-weighting the loss contribution from misclassified examples (i.e., foreground regions).

The focal loss function is defined as follows:

FL(p_t) = -α_t \* (1-p_t)^γ \* log(p_t)

where p_t is the predicted probability of the true class, α_t is a class-specific weighting factor, and γ is a focusing parameter that controls the rate at which the loss decreases as the confidence in the true class increases. The focal loss function is a modification of the standard cross-entropy loss function, which is commonly used in classification tasks. The key innovation of the focal loss function is the introduction of the focusing parameter γ, which allows the model to focus on the most difficult examples (i.e., those with low confidence in the true class) and ignore the easy examples (i.e., those with high confidence in the true class). The initial response to radiation is the induction of DNA damage, which can be in the form of single-strand breaks, double-strand breaks, or base damage (3).
